passages.passageHtml:
The following text is adapted from Mary Shelley's 1818 novel Frankenstein. The narrator, Victor Frankenstein, recalls a childhood memory.

I remember when I was five years old, my mother took me to a forest near our home. [highlight-1]The trees stood like silent giants watching over us.[/highlight-1] I felt safe and small beneath them, as though the world had wrapped itself around me like a blanket.

Researchers have long believed that ancient Egyptians built the pyramids using ramps. However, a 2022 study suggested that at least one pyramid may have been built using a different method: a system of internal tunnels. The study analyzed cracks in the pyramid's stones and found patterns consistent with tunnel construction. [highlight-1]This discovery challenges the long‑held assumption that all pyramids were built using external ramps.[/highlight-1]

In her 2020 memoir, chef Maria Lopez describes growing up in a small Mexican village. She learned to cook by watching her grandmother grind corn by hand. Lopez recalls,

"[highlight-1]The rhythm of the stone against corn was like a heartbeat—steady, ancient, and full of life.[/highlight-1]" This memory inspired her to open a restaurant focused on traditional cooking techniques.

Urban planners in Helsinki have introduced "cool roofs"—roofs painted with reflective white coatings to reduce heat absorption. These roofs lower indoor temperatures by up to 10°C. [highlight-1]The city plans to cover 30% of its rooftops with reflective materials by 2030.[/highlight-1] This initiative is part of Helsinki's goal to become carbon neutral.

The following text is adapted from Langston Hughes's 1930 poem "The Negro Speaks of Rivers."

I've known rivers ancient as the world and older than the flow of human blood in human veins. My soul has grown deep like the rivers. [highlight-1]I bathed in the Euphrates when dawns were young.[/highlight-1]

In a 2023 study, ecologists tracked the movement of sea otters along the California coast. They found that otters spend 70% of their time in kelp forests. [highlight-1]These forests provide shelter from predators and abundant food, such as sea urchins.[/highlight-1] The researchers concluded that protecting kelp forests is critical for otter conservation.

The following text is adapted from Jane Austen's 1815 novel Emma. The narrator describes Mr. Knightley.

Mr. Knightley was a sensible man about seven or eight and thirty. He was not only a very old and intimate friend of the family, but particularly connected with it as the elder brother of Isabella's husband. [highlight-1]He lived about a mile from Highbury, and was a frequent visitor.[/highlight-1] Everyone thought well of him, and he thought well of himself.

Scientists have discovered that some species of octopus can edit their own RNA to adapt to cold temperatures. This ability allows them to modify proteins in their nervous system without changing their DNA. [highlight-1]Before this discovery, researchers believed that only DNA mutations could lead to such adaptations.[/highlight-1] The finding suggests that RNA editing may be more common in intelligent animals than previously thought.

The following text is adapted from Zora Neale Hurston's 1937 novel Their Eyes Were Watching God. Janie, the protagonist, sits under a pear tree.

She saw a bee sinking into the blossom of a pear tree. [highlight-1]The bee's body was dusted with gold pollen, and the flower seemed to welcome him.[/highlight-1] Janie felt a strange ache inside her, as if the tree had whispered a secret she almost understood.

A 2019 law in France required all supermarkets to donate unsold food to charities instead of throwing it away. [highlight-1]The law aimed to reduce food waste while feeding people in need.[/highlight-1] Since the law took effect, food donations have increased by 45%, and supermarkets have reported no significant financial losses.

The following text is adapted from Willa Cather's 1915 novel The Song of the Lark. The protagonist, Thea, is a young singer walking through a canyon.

The walls of the canyon rose straight up, smooth and red as if they had been polished. [highlight-1]The silence was so deep that she could hear her own heartbeat.[/highlight-1] Thea felt as though she had entered a cathedral, a place made for something larger than daily life.

Paleontologists have long debated whether Tyrannosaurus rex was a predator or a scavenger. In a 2021 study, researchers analyzed tooth marks on fossilized bones of herbivorous dinosaurs. [highlight-1]They found that many of the marks had healed over, indicating the prey was alive when bitten.[/highlight-1] This evidence strongly supports the view that T. rex actively hunted at least some of its food.

The following text is adapted from a speech by Frederick Douglass delivered in 1852.

What, to the American slave, is your Fourth of July? I answer: a day that reveals to him, more than all other days in the year, the gross injustice and cruelty to which he is the constant victim. [highlight-1]To him, your celebration is a sham; your boasted liberty, an unholy license; your national greatness, swelling vanity.[/highlight-1] There is not a nation on the earth guilty of practices more shocking and bloody than the people of the United States.

In 2018, the city of Oslo, Norway, began removing parking spaces and adding bike lanes to its city center. [highlight-1]The goal was to reduce car traffic and improve air quality.[/highlight-1] By 2022, the number of cars in the city center had dropped by 30%, and nitrogen dioxide levels fell by 20%. Oslo's approach has since been studied by other cities seeking to reduce emissions.

The following text is adapted from Virginia Woolf's 1925 novel Mrs. Dalloway.

Mrs. Dalloway said she would buy the flowers herself. For Lucy had her work cut out for her. The doors would be taken off their hinges; Rumpelmayer's men were coming. [highlight-1]And then, thought Clarissa Dalloway, what a morning—fresh as if issued to children on a beach.[/highlight-1]

Many historians have attributed the fall of the Roman Empire to a single cause, such as barbarian invasions or economic decline. However, contemporary scholarship emphasizes a combination of factors. [highlight-1]A 2021 study of ancient pollen samples showed that a prolonged drought in the third century CE reduced wheat yields across the Mediterranean.[/highlight-1] This environmental stress likely compounded political and military pressures.

The following text is adapted from Mark Twain's 1883 memoir Life on the Mississippi.

When I was a boy, there was but one permanent ambition among my comrades in our village on the west bank of the Mississippi River. That was, to be a steamboatman. [highlight-1]We had transient ambitions of other sorts, but they were only transient.[/highlight-1] When a steamboat came in sight, the whole town turned out to see it.

Researchers studying memory have found that sleep plays a crucial role in consolidating new information. In one experiment, participants who took a 90-minute nap after learning a list of words recalled 20% more than those who stayed awake. [highlight-1]However, the benefit only appeared when the nap included slow‑wave sleep, the deepest stage.[/highlight-1] This suggests that not all sleep is equally helpful for memory.

The following text is adapted from a 2019 article about urban farming.

Rooftop gardens have become popular in cities like New York and Tokyo. They provide fresh produce, reduce stormwater runoff, and lower building energy costs. [highlight-1]But critics argue that the high installation and maintenance costs make them impractical for low‑income neighborhoods.[/highlight-1] Without subsidies, they say, rooftop farming will remain a luxury for the wealthy.

The following text is adapted from a 1972 speech by environmentalist Rachel Carson.

We stand now where two roads diverge. [highlight-1]One road is the conventional one, paved with synthetic chemicals and quick fixes, promising immediate control over nature.[/highlight-1] But the other road offers a longer, slower journey—one that respects the balance of living systems. The choice is ours to make.

In a 2020 study, economists examined the effect of free public transit on car usage in three European cities. They found that fare‑free buses and trams reduced car trips by only 2‑5%. [highlight-1]Surprisingly, the largest reduction occurred not when transit was free, but when cities added dedicated bus lanes.[/highlight-1] This suggests that travel time, not cost, is the main factor for many commuters.

The following text is adapted from a 1912 essay by Zitkala-Šá (Yankton Dakota writer).

My mother taught me that the prairie grass listened to our footsteps. She said the wind carried our prayers to the stars. [highlight-1]I did not learn these things from books.[/highlight-1] I learned them from the rustling leaves and the silent snow.

Maya cities in the Classic period (250‑900 CE) were not isolated centers. They were linked by a network of raised stone roads called sacbeob (singular sacbe). [highlight-1]One sacbe at the site of Coba stretches over 100 kilometers to the city of Yaxuna.[/highlight-1] This road allowed for trade, military movement, and political alliances between the two cities.

The following text is adapted from a 2023 article on renewable energy.

Solar and wind power are now cheaper than coal in most of the world. But they are intermittent—the sun doesn't always shine, and the wind doesn't always blow. [highlight-1]Energy storage, such as giant batteries, can solve this problem by saving excess power for later use.[/highlight-1] Without storage, renewable energy cannot fully replace fossil fuels.

The following text is adapted from a 1947 letter by Albert Einstein.

A new type of thinking is essential if mankind is to survive and move toward higher levels. [highlight-1]Atomic energy has changed everything save our mode of thinking, and thus we drift toward unparalleled catastrophe.[/highlight-1] We shall require a substantially new manner of thinking if mankind is to survive.

The following text is adapted from a 1962 lecture by philosopher Hannah Arendt.

The modern age has been characterized by a rupture between thought and action. Philosophers have retreated into pure contemplation, while political leaders act without reflection. [highlight-1]This schism, Arendt argues, is not an accident of history but a consequence of the Cartesian obsession with doubt.[/highlight-1] Descartes' method of radical skepticism, by placing the thinking self in isolation, severed the individual from the common world. The result, Arendt warns, is a politics without meaning and a philosophy without responsibility.

Astronomers have long assumed that planet formation occurs primarily in the gas‑rich disks around young stars. However, recent observations from the James Webb Space Telescope have identified what appear to be planetary embryos in a disk that is unusually poor in heavy elements. [highlight-1]These embryos, if confirmed, would challenge the prevailing model because that model requires a minimum metallicity for efficient planet formation.[/highlight-1] The discovery team cautions that alternative explanations, such as background galaxy contamination, have not yet been ruled out.

The following text is adapted from a 1923 essay by W.E.B. Du Bois.

The problem of the twentieth century is the problem of the color line. But this line is not fixed; it moves and shifts with economic forces. [highlight-1]Where capital flows, the color line follows, not as a natural boundary but as a tool of exploitation.[/highlight-1] Thus, the struggle for racial justice cannot be separated from the struggle against capitalism. To attack one without the other is to fight shadows.

In a 2022 meta‑analysis of 47 studies, psychologists examined whether "power posing" (adopting expansive postures) actually affects hormone levels and risk‑taking behavior. The analysis found no consistent evidence that power posing changes testosterone or cortisol, nor that it influences behavioral outcomes. [highlight-1]However, the authors caution that the original studies varied widely in methodology, and some lacked sufficient statistical power to detect small effects.[/highlight-1] This means that a weak effect cannot be definitively ruled out, though the current evidence does not support strong claims.

The following text is adapted from a 1956 speech by physicist J. Robert Oppenheimer.

We have learned to make things that work, but we have not learned to use them wisely. The atomic bomb is the most obvious example, but the same applies to many lesser technologies. [highlight-1]It is not that scientists are immoral; it is that morality has not kept pace with capability.[/highlight-1] This lag is the central crisis of our time. To solve it, we need not more knowledge but more wisdom.

Art historian Jennifer L. Roberts argues that slow looking—prolonged, patient observation of a single artwork—is essential for understanding complex visual works. In her teaching, she requires students to spend three hours looking at a single painting before writing about it. [highlight-1]Most students initially resist this exercise, finding it tedious and unproductive.[/highlight-1] Yet Roberts contends that the discomfort of slowness forces viewers to move beyond first impressions and to notice details, relationships, and ambiguities that rapid scanning misses. This practice, she says, cultivates a form of attention that is increasingly rare in the digital age.

The following text is adapted from a 2015 environmental economics study.

Subsidies for renewable energy are often criticized for being costly. But a more subtle problem is that they can create perverse incentives: in some markets, solar farms have been built on prime agricultural land, displacing food production. [highlight-1]This land‑use conflict suggests that renewable subsidies should be designed to prioritize marginal lands, such as rooftops or brownfields.[/highlight-1] Without such targeting, green energy policies may inadvertently harm other social goods.

The following text is adapted from a 1929 novel by Nella Larsen.

Helga Crane sat alone in her room, watching the snow fall past the window. She had left the South to escape its suffocating certainties, but the North offered only a different kind of cage. [highlight-1]Her job at the insurance company required her to smile at white customers while pretending not to notice their suspicion.[/highlight-1] At night, she read poems by Langston Hughes and imagined a life where her skin was not a problem to be managed. But morning always returned, with its dull weight of endurance.

In a 2018 study of corporate boardrooms, sociologists observed that women who speak assertively are often labeled "aggressive," while men using identical language are called "decisive." The researchers argue that this double bind discourages women from advocating for themselves or their ideas. However, a follow‑up experiment found that when the same assertive statements were attributed to a female executive with a documented record of success, the negative labels disappeared. [highlight-1]This suggests that competence can override gender bias, but only for women who have already proven themselves—a catch‑22 for those just starting their careers.[/highlight-1]

The following text is adapted from a 1978 book by Edward Said, Orientalism.

The Western study of the "Orient" has never been a neutral scholarly pursuit. It has been a political and cultural project, constructing the East as backward, sensual, and despotic in order to justify colonial domination. [highlight-1]One might object that some Orientalists, like Sir William Jones, genuinely admired Eastern cultures and learned their languages with respect.[/highlight-1] But admiration, Said counters, is not the same as equality; even the sympathetic scholar frames the Orient as an object of study, not a subject of history.

questions.questionHtml: Which choice best describes the function of the bolded sentence in the text as a whole?

options.A: It emphasizes the narratorʼs fear of being watched.
options.B: It suggests that the narrator felt threatened by the forest.
options.C: It conveys the narratorʼs sense of comfort and wonder in nature.
options.D: It introduces a conflict between the narrator and his mother.

questions.explanationHtml:
• The bolded sentence uses a simile (“like silent giants watching over us”) and is followed by the narrator feeling “safe and small” and “wrapped” by the world. This creates a tone of comfort and awe, not fear.
  • A and B are traps because “watching” might seem threatening, but the context shows the narrator feels protected.
  • D is incorrect because no conflict with the mother is mentioned.

questions.questionHtml: Which choice best states the function of the bolded sentence?

options.A: It summarizes the main finding of the study.
options.B: It questions whether the studyʼs methods were reliable.
options.C: It introduces a new theory about pyramid construction.
options.D: It rejects the idea that ramps were used at all.

questions.explanationHtml:
• The bolded sentence directly states what the discovery does—challenge a long‑held assumption. This summarizes the study’s implication.
  • C is a trap because the new theory (internal tunnels) is introduced earlier; the bolded sentence explains the impact.
  • B is incorrect — no reliability concerns are raised.
  • D is incorrect because it says “all pyramids,” but the study only challenges the assumption for one pyramid.

questions.questionHtml: Which choice best describes the function of the bolded sentence?

options.A: It illustrates how Lopez learned to appreciate modern cooking tools.
options.B: It shows the emotional connection Lopez felt to a traditional practice.
options.C: It explains why Lopez decided to leave her village.
options.D: It criticizes the inefficiency of manual food preparation.

questions.explanationHtml:
• The simile comparing grinding corn to a heartbeat shows deep emotional resonance and connection to tradition.
  • A is a trap — no modern tools are mentioned.
  • C is incorrect — the memoir is about her inspiration, not leaving.
  • D is incorrect — no criticism is present; the tone is reverent.

questions.questionHtml: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

options.A: To argue that other cities should adopt Helsinki's policies.
options.B: To explain the science behind reflective roof coatings.
options.C: To describe Helsinki's strategy and target for reducing heat using cool roofs.
options.D: To compare cool roofs to other cooling methods like green roofs.

questions.explanationHtml:
• The text explains what cool roofs are, their effect, and Helsinki's specific goal (30% by 2030) as part of a carbon‑neutral plan.
  • A is incorrect — no argument or recommendation is made.
  • B is too narrow — the text focuses on the plan, not just the science.
  • D is incorrect — no comparison is made.

questions.questionHtml: Which choice best describes the function of the bolded line in the poem?

options.A: It provides a specific example of the speaker's connection to ancient rivers.
options.B: It shifts the poem's tone from reflective to angry.
options.C: It introduces a historical fact about the Euphrates River.
options.D: It contrasts the speaker's experience with modern life.

questions.explanationHtml:
• The speaker claims to have known ancient rivers; the bolded line gives a concrete, poetic example (bathing in the Euphrates at the dawn of time) to support that claim.
  • B is incorrect — the tone remains reflective and proud.
  • C is a trap — the line is metaphorical, not a historical claim.
  • D is incorrect — no contrast with modern life is made.

questions.questionHtml: Which choice best describes the function of the bolded sentence?

options.A: It explains why otters prefer kelp forests over other habitats.
options.B: It argues that sea urchins should be removed from kelp forests.
options.C: It introduces a new predator of sea otters.
options.D: It criticizes previous studies for ignoring kelp forests.

questions.explanationHtml:
• The bolded sentence gives two reasons (shelter and food) why otters spend so much time in kelp forests, directly explaining their preference.
  • B is incorrect — no removal is suggested.
  • C is incorrect — no predator is named.
  • D is incorrect — no criticism of prior studies is made.

questions.questionHtml: Which choice best describes the function of the bolded sentence?

options.A: It shows that Mr. Knightley is distant and unfriendly.
options.B: It provides a logistical detail that explains his frequent presence.
options.C: It suggests that Mr. Knightley dislikes his own home.
options.D: It contrasts Mr. Knightley's character with others in Highbury.

questions.explanationHtml:
• The bolded sentence explains where he lives (a mile away) and that he visits often, which helps readers understand his accessibility to the family.
  • A is a trap — “lived about a mile” is not far; “frequent visitor” shows closeness.
  • C is incorrect — no dislike of home is mentioned.
  • D is incorrect — no contrast is drawn.

questions.questionHtml: Which choice best states the function of the bolded sentence?

options.A: It identifies a flaw in the method of earlier studies.
options.B: It explains how RNA editing affects octopus behavior.
options.C: It highlights how the discovery challenges prior scientific beliefs.
options.D: It compares RNA editing to DNA mutation rates.

questions.explanationHtml:
• The bolded sentence directly states what researchers believed before the discovery, setting up the contrast that the new finding challenges that belief.
  • A is incorrect — no flaw in methods is mentioned.
  • B is incorrect — behavior is not discussed.
  • D is a trap — no comparison of rates is made.

questions.questionHtml: Which choice best describes the function of the bolded sentence?

options.A: It suggests that the bee is damaging the flower.
options.B: It uses nature to symbolize harmony and longing.
options.C: It explains why Janie is afraid of insects.
options.D: It introduces a conflict between Janie and the tree.

questions.explanationHtml:
• The bolded sentence shows a gentle, mutual interaction between bee and flower (pollen, welcome), which parallels Janie's emotional “ache” and longing for connection.
  • A is a trap — “welcome” suggests the opposite of damage.
  • C is incorrect — no fear is shown.
  • D is incorrect — no conflict is present.

questions.questionHtml: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

options.A: To argue that other countries should pass similar food waste laws.
options.B: To describe the goal of a French food waste law and its positive outcomes.
options.C: To compare French supermarkets' waste levels to those in other countries.
options.D: To criticize supermarkets for wasting food before 2019.

questions.explanationHtml:
• The text states the law's goal (bolded) and then gives two outcomes (increased donations, no financial losses).
  • A is incorrect — no argument or recommendation is made.
  • C is incorrect — no comparison is made.
  • D is a trap — no criticism is expressed; the tone is neutral.

questions.questionHtml: Which choice best describes the function of the bolded sentence in the text as a whole?

options.A: It contrasts Thea's internal turmoil with the calmness of the canyon.
options.B: It emphasizes the profound stillness of the setting, heightening Thea's sense of awe.
options.C: It suggests that Thea is afraid of being alone in the canyon.
options.D: It indicates that Thea is physically exhausted from her walk.

questions.explanationHtml:
• The bolded sentence highlights the extreme quiet (“hear her own heartbeat”), which reinforces the cathedral‑like, sacred atmosphere described in the following sentence.
  • A is a trap — no internal turmoil is mentioned.
  • C is incorrect — no fear is suggested.
  • D is incorrect — exhaustion is not implied.

questions.questionHtml: Which choice best describes the function of the bolded sentence in the text as a whole?

options.A: It summarizes a widely accepted conclusion about T. rex behavior.
options.B: It introduces a new hypothesis that the rest of the text will challenge.
options.C: It provides specific evidence that supports one side of a scientific debate.
options.D: It questions the reliability of fossil tooth marks as evidence.

questions.explanationHtml:
• The bolded sentence gives direct evidence (healed bite marks) that T. rex attacked living prey, supporting the predator hypothesis.
  • A is incorrect — the conclusion is not widely accepted; there is a debate.
  • B is a trap — the text supports, not challenges, the evidence.
  • D is incorrect — no reliability question is raised.

questions.questionHtml: Which choice best describes the function of the bolded sentence in the speech?

options.A: It concedes that the nation has made progress toward liberty.
options.B: It lists three specific ways the holiday is meaningful to enslaved people.
options.C: It uses parallel structure to condemn the hypocrisy of celebrating freedom while slavery exists.
options.D: It shifts the tone from angry to hopeful.

questions.explanationHtml:
• The bolded sentence uses repetition (“your... your... your”) to attack the contradiction between American ideals and the reality of slavery.
  • A is incorrect — no concession is made.
  • B is a trap — the sentence does not describe what the holiday “means” to enslaved people but rather exposes its falseness.
  • D is incorrect — the tone remains critical and angry.

questions.questionHtml: Which choice best describes the function of the bolded sentence in the text?

options.A: It explains the reason behind Oslo's policy changes.
options.B: It presents a counterargument to the city's transportation plan.
options.C: It describes an unexpected outcome of the policy.
options.D: It compares Oslo's results to those of other cities.

questions.explanationHtml:
• The bolded sentence states the intended purpose of removing parking and adding bike lanes, which is to reduce traffic and improve air quality.
  • B is incorrect — no counterargument is given.
  • C is a trap — the outcomes are presented later, but the bolded sentence gives the goal, not an outcome.
  • D is incorrect — comparison comes later; the bolded sentence does not compare.

questions.questionHtml: Which choice best describes the function of the bolded sentence?

options.A: It shifts from practical planning to a moment of personal, poetic reflection.
options.B: It reveals Mrs. Dalloway's frustration with the household staff.
options.C: It introduces a flashback to a childhood memory.
options.D: It contrasts the busy morning with a quiet evening.

questions.explanationHtml:
• The first part of the passage deals with tasks (flowers, doors, workers). The bolded sentence switches to a lyrical thought about the morning's freshness, showing Clarissa's inner perspective.
  • B is incorrect — no frustration with Lucy is shown.
  • C is a trap — the comparison to children on a beach is a simile, not a flashback.
  • D is incorrect — no evening is mentioned.

questions.questionHtml: Which choice best describes the function of the bolded sentence?

options.A: It introduces a new, previously unknown cause of Rome's fall.
options.B: It provides concrete data supporting a multifactorial explanation.
options.C: It argues against the importance of barbarian invasions.
options.D: It summarizes the main argument of the study.

questions.explanationHtml:
• The bolded sentence offers specific scientific evidence (pollen data, drought, reduced wheat) that supports the idea that multiple factors (environmental, political, military) contributed to Rome's fall.
  • A is incorrect — drought was not “previously unknown” to historians.
  • C is a trap — the sentence does not argue against barbarian invasions; it adds another factor.
  • D is incorrect — the study's main argument is not summarized here; evidence is presented.

questions.questionHtml: Which choice best describes the function of the bolded sentence?

options.A: It diminishes the importance of other childhood dreams to emphasize the dominance of becoming a steamboatman.
options.B: It suggests that the narrator's friends were easily distracted.
options.C: It lists several alternative careers the boys considered.
options.D: It reveals that the narrator eventually gave up on becoming a steamboatman.

questions.explanationHtml:
• The bolded sentence contrasts fleeting ambitions with the permanent ambition of being a steamboatman, strengthening the central idea.
  • B is a trap — “transient” means short‑lived, not easily distracted.
  • C is incorrect — no specific careers are listed.
  • D is incorrect — the narrator does not reveal his own outcome.

questions.questionHtml: Which choice best describes the function of the bolded sentence?

options.A: It introduces a limitation of the study's findings.
options.B: It states the main conclusion of the experiment.
options.C: It contrasts the nap group with the wake group.
options.D: It describes the method used to measure recall.

questions.explanationHtml:
• The bolded sentence adds a condition (“only when the nap included slow‑wave sleep”), which limits the generalizability of the benefit.
  • B is incorrect — the main conclusion is in the final sentence.
  • C is a trap — the contrast is made earlier; this sentence refines the contrast.
  • D is incorrect — no method is described.

questions.questionHtml: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?

options.A: It presents a problem, then offers a solution.
options.B: It lists benefits of a practice, then acknowledges a drawback.
options.C: It compares two different farming methods.
options.D: It defends a practice against common criticisms.

questions.explanationHtml:
• The first part gives positive aspects of rooftop gardens (produce, runoff reduction, energy savings). The bolded sentence and following sentence introduce a negative aspect (cost, impracticality for low‑income areas).
  • A is incorrect — no solution is offered.
  • C is incorrect — no comparison to other farming methods.
  • D is a trap — the text does not defend; it presents both sides neutrally.

questions.questionHtml: Which choice best describes the function of the bolded sentence?

options.A: It describes the less desirable path in vivid, critical language.
options.B: It praises the efficiency of modern chemical solutions.
options.C: It explains the scientific basis for pest control.
options.D: It suggests that both roads lead to the same destination.

questions.explanationHtml:
• The bolded sentence characterizes the conventional road with negative connotations (“synthetic,” “quick fixes”) to make it unappealing, contrasting with the respectful alternative.
  • B is incorrect — the language is critical, not praising.
  • C is incorrect — no scientific explanation is given.
  • D is a trap — the roads lead to different outcomes, implied by the contrast.

questions.questionHtml: Which choice best describes the function of the bolded sentence?

options.A: It presents a finding that contradicts what the reader might expect.
options.B: It restates the study's hypothesis.
options.C: It criticizes the methodology of the study.
options.D: It provides a cost-benefit analysis of free transit.

questions.explanationHtml:
• The word “Surprisingly” signals that the finding (dedicated lanes > free fare) goes against expectations that cost is the biggest barrier.
  • B is incorrect — no hypothesis is stated earlier.
  • C is incorrect — no criticism of methods.
  • D is a trap — no cost‑benefit analysis is given.

questions.questionHtml: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?

options.A: It contrasts two different methods of learning.
options.B: It argues that oral tradition is superior to written history.
options.C: It describes a specific event from the narrator's childhood.
options.D: It presents a series of scientific facts about nature.

questions.explanationHtml:
• The first two sentences give examples of learning from nature through a mother's teaching. The last two sentences explicitly contrast that with learning from books, emphasizing nature as the source.
  • B is a trap — the text implies value but does not explicitly argue superiority.
  • C is incorrect — no single event is described.
  • D is incorrect — the statements are spiritual, not scientific.

questions.questionHtml: Which choice best describes the function of the bolded sentence?

options.A: It provides an example that illustrates the scale of Maya road networks.
options.B: It argues that Coba was the most important Maya city.
options.C: It compares Coba's road to those of other ancient civilizations.
options.D: It suggests that sacbeob were used only for religious ceremonies.

questions.explanationHtml:
• The bolded sentence gives a specific, long‑distance example to support the general claim that Maya cities were linked by roads.
  • B is incorrect — no claim of importance is made.
  • C is a trap — no comparison to other civilizations.
  • D is incorrect — the next sentence lists trade, military, and politics, not just religion.

questions.questionHtml: Which choice best describes the function of the bolded sentence?

options.A: It identifies a major drawback of solar and wind power.
options.B: It proposes a solution to a limitation of renewable energy.
options.C: It explains why coal remains popular in some regions.
options.D: It compares battery storage costs to fuel costs.

questions.explanationHtml:
• The bolded sentence directly addresses the intermittency problem mentioned earlier by offering storage as a solution.
  • A is incorrect — the drawback (intermittency) is stated in the previous sentence.
  • C is a trap — coal is not discussed after the first sentence.
  • D is incorrect — no cost comparison is given.

questions.questionHtml: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?

options.A: It states a problem, then repeats the same problem in different words.
options.B: It offers a historical overview of atomic energy.
options.C: It compares two different types of thinking.
options.D: It presents a solution and then explains why it will work.

questions.explanationHtml:
• The first sentence says new thinking is needed. The bolded sentence explains why (atomic energy + old thinking = catastrophe). The final sentence restates the need for new thinking. The structure is problem‑elaboration‑repetition for emphasis.
  • B is incorrect — no historical overview.
  • C is a trap — only one type (old) is implied; new is what's needed.
  • D is incorrect — no solution is presented, only the need for one.

questions.questionHtml: Which choice best describes the function of the bolded sentence in the text as a whole?

options.A: It introduces a historical claim that the following sentences will disprove.
options.B: It presents Arendt's own diagnosis of the cause of a problem described earlier.
options.C: It summarizes the main argument of the passage before offering a counterexample.
options.D: It shifts the focus from political to epistemological concerns.

questions.explanationHtml:
• The first two sentences describe a problem (rupture between thought and action). The bolded sentence states Arendt's explanation for this problem: it is a consequence of Cartesian doubt. The following sentences elaborate on that diagnosis.
  • A is a trap — the following sentences support, not disprove, the claim.
  • C is incorrect — no counterexample follows.
  • D is incorrect — the focus remains on the thought‑action divide, not exclusively epistemology.

questions.questionHtml: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

options.A: To report a discovery that, if verified, would undermine a long‑standing theory in astronomy.
options.B: To argue that the James Webb Space Telescope is the only instrument capable of detecting planetary embryos.
options.C: To compare the metallicity requirements of different planet formation models.
options.D: To explain why background galaxy contamination is the most likely explanation for the observations.

questions.explanationHtml:
• The text presents a potential discovery that contradicts the prevailing model’s requirement for high metallicity. The bolded sentence explicitly states the challenge. The final sentence adds a caveat, but the main purpose remains reporting a possible theory‑disrupting finding.
  • B is incorrect — the text does not argue exclusivity of JWST.
  • C is a trap — no comparison of models is provided.
  • D is incorrect — contamination is mentioned as an alternative, not the most likely explanation.

questions.questionHtml: Which choice best describes the function of the bolded sentence in the text as a whole?

options.A: It offers a concrete example of racial injustice in industrial settings.
options.B: It asserts a causal relationship between economic and racial dynamics.
options.C: It rejects the idea that the color line is a product of natural differences.
options.D: It introduces a counterargument that the following sentence refutes.

questions.explanationHtml:
• The bolded sentence states that capital flow determines the location of the color line, and that the color line is a “tool of exploitation” (i.e., economic). This asserts a causal link between capitalism and racial hierarchy.
  • A is incorrect — no concrete example is given.
  • C is a trap — the sentence does reject natural boundary, but that is secondary; the main function is causal assertion.
  • D is incorrect — the following sentence agrees with and extends the claim.

questions.questionHtml: Which choice best describes the function of the bolded sentence?

options.A: It undermines the meta-analysis's own conclusion by highlighting methodological flaws.
options.B: It provides a nuanced qualification of the null findings reported earlier.
options.C: It shifts the focus from physiological to psychological effects of power posing.
options.D: It argues that future research should abandon randomized controlled trials.

questions.explanationHtml:
• The meta‑analysis found no consistent evidence (null result). The bolded sentence adds a caveat: because of methodological variation and low power, a small effect cannot be ruled out. This qualifies the null finding without overturning it.
  • A is a trap — it does not undermine the conclusion; it contextualizes it.
  • C is incorrect — no shift in focus occurs.
  • D is incorrect — no abandonment of methods is advocated.

questions.questionHtml: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?

options.A: It identifies a problem, offers two possible causes, and then advocates for a solution that combines both.
options.B: It states a general observation, provides a specific example, diagnoses a cause, and proposes a remedy.
options.C: It compares two different historical periods and argues that the present is uniquely dangerous.
options.D: It criticizes scientists for their moral failures and then calls for religious education.

questions.explanationHtml:
• The structure: observation (we make things but don't use wisely) → example (atomic bomb) → diagnosis (morality lagging) → remedy (need wisdom, not knowledge).
  • A is a trap — two causes are not offered; one cause is given.
  • C is incorrect — no historical comparison.
  • D is incorrect — scientists are not blamed; the lag is societal.

questions.questionHtml: Which choice best describes the function of the bolded sentence?

options.A: It provides evidence that Roberts's method is ineffective for most learners.
options.B: It introduces a counterpoint that the rest of the paragraph will resolve.
options.C: It explains why Roberts chose to focus on painting rather than sculpture.
options.D: It summarizes the main conclusion of Roberts's research.

questions.explanationHtml:
• The bolded sentence presents student resistance as an obstacle or opposing viewpoint. The following sentences (starting with “Yet”) show how Roberts addresses or reframes that resistance. This is a classic counterpoint‑response structure.
  • A is incorrect — the text does not conclude the method is ineffective.
  • C is a trap — no comparison to sculpture.
  • D is incorrect — the conclusion is about the value of slow looking, not student resistance.

questions.questionHtml: Which choice best describes the function of the bolded sentence?

options.A: It states a conclusion that follows from the preceding evidence and supports the following recommendation.
options.B: It introduces an alternative explanation for land-use conflicts that the text will reject.
options.C: It questions the validity of the criticism mentioned in the first sentence.
options.D: It provides a counterexample to the claim that subsidies are costly.

questions.explanationHtml:
• The evidence (solar farms on agricultural land) leads to the claim in the bolded sentence (“suggests that subsidies should be designed...”); the following sentence explains the consequence. The bolded sentence acts as an intermediate conclusion that supports a policy recommendation.
  • B is incorrect — no alternative explanation is introduced.
  • C is a trap — the bolded sentence does not question the “costly” criticism; it adds a new problem.
  • D is incorrect — no counterexample to cost criticism is given.

questions.questionHtml: Which choice best describes the function of the bolded sentence in the text as a whole?

options.A: It illustrates the psychological strain of the protagonist's daily work environment.
options.B: It contrasts Helga's professional life with her private reading habits.
options.C: It introduces a secondary character who will become important later.
options.D: It explains why Helga left the South for the North.

questions.explanationHtml:
• The bolded sentence gives a concrete example of the “different kind of cage” mentioned in the previous sentence: the emotional labor of smiling while enduring suspicion. This illustrates the internal conflict and strain of her work life.
  • B is a trap — the contrast is implied but the sentence's primary function is to show strain, not contrast per se.
  • C is incorrect — no secondary character is introduced.
  • D is incorrect — the reason for leaving the South is given earlier (“suffocating certainties”), not in this sentence.

questions.questionHtml: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?

options.A: It presents a phenomenon, discusses an explanation, and then introduces a countervailing finding that complicates the explanation.
options.B: It states a hypothesis, describes two experiments that test it, and concludes that the hypothesis is false.
options.C: It offers a critique of corporate hiring practices and then proposes a solution.
options.D: It compares the experiences of male and female executives across three different industries.

questions.explanationHtml:
• Phenomenon (women labeled aggressive) → explanation (double bind) → follow‑up finding (competence removes negative labels, but only for proven women) → complication (catch‑22 for beginners).
  • B is incorrect — no hypothesis is stated, and the conclusion is not that the hypothesis is false.
  • C is a trap — no solution is proposed.
  • D is incorrect — no industry comparison.

questions.questionHtml: Which choice best describes the function of the bolded sentence?

options.A: It presents a potential objection to Said's argument, which the next sentence rebuts.
options.B: It supports Said's claim by providing a positive example of an Orientalist.
options.C: It shifts the focus from political motives to linguistic methodology.
options.D: It concedes that Orientalism has no harmful effects.

questions.explanationHtml:
• The first two sentences state Said's argument (Orientalism as political project). The bolded sentence introduces a possible counterexample (“one might object... genuinely admired”). The following sentence (“But admiration...”) directly rebuts that objection. This is a classic concession‑rebuttal structure.
  • B is incorrect — the sentence is not supporting Said; it's presenting a challenge.
  • C is a trap — no methodological shift occurs.
  • D is incorrect — no concession about harmlessness is made.
